articles.author: Asermu
articles.description:
I run Asermu, a novel-writing app built with Next.js and deployed as a Docker image on Railway. I added Sentry a while ago. The dashboard stayed quiet, and I took that as good news.
It wasn't. Today I found that server-side Sentry had never started in production. Not once.
I keep a flag-gated test route that reports a test error to Sentry on purpose. On the server runtime it returned:
{ "sent": true, "runtime": "nodejs", "eventId": "309ea78...", "flushOk": false }

captureException happily handed back an event id. But Sentry.flush() returned false, and nothing arrived in Sentry. The same test on the edge runtime returned flushOk: true, and its event showed up in Sentry.
In 90 days, Sentry had received exactly one event: my own edge test. Zero real server errors is not the same as zero erro…
articles.title: Sentry never ran on my Next.js server, and the dashboard looked fine

articles.author: Syed Abdul Hanan
articles.description:
How one artificial neuron makes a decision, and how it fixes itself when it's wrong.
In 1958, psychologist Frank Rosenblatt unveiled the perceptron at the Cornell Aeronautical Laboratory. The press got excited. The New York Times wrote that the Navy expected it to one day walk, talk, see, and write.
It couldn't do any of that. But it introduced an idea that every modern neural network still uses: a machine that improves by fixing its own mistakes.
Under the hood, a perceptron is a single artificial neuron. It does three things:
It takes some inputs, like x₁ and x₂.
It multiplies each input by a weight (w₁ and w₂) and adds them up.
It compares the sum with a threshold, written θ (theta).
If the sum clears the threshold, the perceptron outputs 1. Otherwise, it outputs 0. That's the whole dec…
articles.title: The perceptron: the 1958 machine that learned from its mistakes

articles.author: Theodore Creates Co.
articles.description:
If you build with Cursor, Claude Code, Copilot or Windsurf, you've probably had at least one of these happen:
You asked for a small fix and the agent "tidied up" four other files.
An API key ended up hard-coded in a component, or behind a NEXT_PUBLIC_ prefix where every visitor can read it.
A new API route works perfectly, for every user, including the ones who shouldn't see that record.
The agent tried the same broken fix five times, each one making things a bit worse.
Tests were "fixed" by skipping them.
None of this is the model being stupid. It's the model doing exactly what it was asked, with no idea what you consider off-limits. The fix is cheap: give it a short, clear set of house rules it reads at the start of every session.
Most AI coding tools now read a plain Markdown instructio…
